evidence.paraphrase: Janamejaya asks Vyāsa about Śatākṣī. Durgama, son of Ruru of Hiraṇyākṣa family, seeks Vedic mantras and power through a thousand years of air-only Brahmā worship; Brahmā agrees. Loss of rites weakens gods; drought lasts a hundred years. Brahmins pray to the Goddess in the Himalaya. Her many eyes shed rain-restoring tears for nine nights; she carries plant food in one hand.

narrative_events.details: Vyāsa answers Janamejaya: Ruru’s son Durgama, of Hiraṇyākṣa’s family, plans to obtain Vedas so gods lose offerings. He worships Brahmā in the Himalaya for1,000years on air. Brahmā offers a boon; Durgama requests all Vedic mantras of gods/Brahmins and conquering strength; Brahmā agrees.
narrative_events.outcome: Brahmins forget Vedas and Vedic rites cease.

narrative_events.details: Without Vedic rites gods weaken. Durgama attacks Amarāvatī; gods flee into Sumeru caves. Rain ceases for100years, drying water and killing people and animals. Brahmins fast and pray to the Mother in the Himalaya.

The Goddess appears with innumerable eyes and four arms holding bow, arrows, lotus and food. She weeps for nine nights, restoring water; many-eyed Śatākṣī distributes vegetables, roots and fruits until crops return, and grass for animals, receiving the designation Śākambharī.

Messengers tell Durgama of the rescue; he surrounds the defenders with1,000akṣauhiṇīs. A luminous enclosure protects gods and Brahmins while the Goddess fights outside. Arrow clouds darken the sky; frictional fire illuminates it. Fourteen named Śaktis,10,000Guhya Kālikās, groups of32and64and innumerable others emerge and fight.
narrative_events.outcome: After the Śaktis destroy100akṣauhiṇīs, instruments sound and Durgama first confronts them; ten days of fighting destroy all his troops.

narrative_events.details: On day11 red-clothed Durgama advances in his chariot, overcomes Śaktis and faces the Goddess for two praharas. Her15arrows strike four horses, charioteer, two eyes, two arms, flag, and five strike his heart. He vomits blood and dies; his luminosity merges into the Goddess.
narrative_events.outcome: Durgama dies; this is no surrender.

narrative_events.details: Gods including Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva praise the victor. She hands the Vedas to the Brahmins and instructs that they be guarded as parts of her body. She connects Durgā with killing Durgama and names Durgā/Śatākṣī remembrance as liberating from Māyā; the many-eye naming explanation occurred earlier. She enjoins both Suras and Asuras to serve her alone and read her deeds, then disappears. Vyāsa directs secrecy for this mystery and promises daily devoted hearing fulfills wishes and ends in honor in Devī Loka.

Aruṇa lives in a nether Daitya city, then undertakes Brahmā worship beside Ganges in Himalaya. Four successive10,000year stages use dry leaves, water drops, air and finally no food; he repeats Gāyatrī continuously. His ascetic heat threatens worlds; gods petition Brahmā. Brahmā appears with Gāyatrī and four Vedas.

Aruṇa first requests immortality. Brahmā refuses an impossible boon and says Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva too are mortal. Aruṇa revises the request to the specified war/weapon/sex/limb-category death exclusions and strength to conquer gods. Brahmā assents.
narrative_events.outcome: A qualified boon, not universal immortality, is granted.

narrative_events.details: Aruṇa gathers nether Daityas, sends a messenger to Indra and conquers heaven, taking forms/offices of sun, moon, Yama, Agni and others through ascetic power. Gods seek counsel with Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva at Kailāsa.

A heavenly voice directs worship of the world Queen and identifies cessation of Gāyatrī repetition as the condition making Aruṇa killable. Indra sends Bṛhaspati; gods perform Devī sacrifice and Māyā-bīja worship. Bṛhaspati approaches as a muni and argues that sharing the gods’ Goddess worship undermines Aruṇa’s hostility. Aruṇa abandons Gāyatrī through pride and loses strength; Bṛhaspati reports success.
narrative_events.outcome: Gods continue worship; a long interval of unspecified duration follows.

narrative_events.details: After continued worship Bhrāmarī appears with diverse garments and ornaments, bees in her fists and garland, and boon/fearlessness gestures. Bee sound is associated with Hrīm. Gods offer an extended hymn, then describe Aruṇa’s boon and injuries. Hymnic names are attributed praise, not separate narrated births.

Bhrāmarī releases bees/hornets from every side. Their multitude covers the world and attacks the Daityas’ chests. The text denies the foes time or capacity to fight, wield weapons or speak; principal Daityas perish immediately. Bees return to the Goddess; gods rejoice with praise, music and dance.
narrative_events.outcome: Aruṇa’s forces perish; no negotiated surrender.

narrative_events.details: The Goddess grants separate boons to the gods, whose individual contents are not specified here, and grants their express request for unshakeable devotion. She disappears; Nārāyaṇa concludes with liberation promised for hearing the account.

Gods distressed after Satī’s departure and by Tāraka worship the Goddess. They report Brahmā’s provision that Śiva’s son kills Tāraka, and request her incarnation and steadfast devotion. She promises that her Śakti will be Gaurī in Himālaya’s house, Śiva’s wife and mother of the slayer. These are promises here, not a birth already narrated. Himālaya praises the favor and asks for her Vedāntic true nature and knowledge with devotion.

The Goddess identifies her precreation self with consciousness and Brahman and describes inherent Māyā, its concealment and liberation functions, and dependence of cosmos on her Śakti. The discourse moves through elements, subtle/causal/gross bodies, organs and prāṇas, and Jīva/Īśvara distinctions. This is attributed doctrine; translator parenthetical explanations and potentially corrupt organ locations need Sanskrit checking.

Vyāsa answers with the Goddess’s own created residence, Maṇidvīpa, above the other divine worlds and serving as an umbrella over them. Sudhā ocean surrounds it; the outer iron enclosure is seven yojanas, with four guarded gates receiving divine visitors and vehicles. The next enclosure is white copper in this English witness.
narrative_events.outcome: Further gardens, seasonal rulers and enclosures follow.
